name: soundness
description: "The patterns by which safe Rust over C has reached undefined behaviour in Crustify's campaigns, each with what prevents it and which check catches it, and how the catalogue grows from proven findings. Read before analysing, binding or porting any item, before writing its UB tests, and when reviewing for UB or contracts."
---

# Soundness patterns

The ways a binding or a port of C has let safe Rust reach undefined behaviour, or met a
memory-safety defect of the C that it had to keep out of its safe API. Every pattern here
has a proven finding of a campaign behind it: the catalogue records what went wrong, not
what could. An item's analysis asks of each pattern whether the item can meet it, and a
review for UB or contracts reads the item against the same list, so that a defect one
module met is not met again in the next.

## 1. Patterns

Each pattern has an id, which a finding's report names. What prevents a pattern is stated
as what the Rust does; [`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md) and [`porting`](../porting/SKILL.md)
give the routes that do it.

### 1.1 Values the C trusts

| id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `unchecked-arithmetic` | The C computes with a value a safe caller controls and does not check it: a signed overflow, a shift, a size that wraps with its header, a zero divisor. | The Rust checks the value's range before the call, sizes past `isize::MAX` included, and refuses what the C would compute wrongly. | UBSan, review |
| `diverging-precheck` | A check in Rust repeats the C's parsing or evaluation and differs from what the C then computes. | The Rust validates the exact value the C will use, or computes the result itself and hands the C only that. | UBSan |
| `degenerate-input` | The C reads out of bounds on an input its own validation accepts, such as an empty string beside others or a null pointer for a string. | Every wrapper that can route the input to that reader refuses or normalises it, the indirect routes included. | ASan |
| `variant-mismatch` | A tagged, variable-size value of another variant than its container expects is passed on, and the C sizes its buffers by the container's. | The Rust compares the value's variant with the container's before any call that looks it up or formats it. | ASan |

### 1.2 Memory and ownership

| id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `size-known-to-c` | Only the C knows an object's true size or layout: an opaque type, a pointer a tag types, a base struct its callbacks read past, an array sized by a count. Rust builds it too small or types it wrongly. | Such an object is allocated through the C alone, a tagged pointer is typed only where its tag is vouched for, and an object whose callbacks read more than Rust built is refused. | ASan, review |
| `hidden-dependency` | A handle, a lent pointer or a callback outlives something it depends on without showing it: a parent it points back to, a global the program may close, lent memory the C copied into a second slot. | The handle's lifetime is tied to that owner, or it keeps the owner alive; a pointer the C stores is bounded by its longest-lived reader. | ASan, Miri, review |
| `failure-leaves-state` | A failure path of the C, most often a failed allocation, leaves an object uninitialised, freed, wrongly sized or half written and still returns, sometimes reporting success. | The Rust trusts nothing the C leaves after a failure: it validates outputs again, does not reuse the object, and composes the operation itself where the C's error path is unsafe. | ASan, UBSan, review |
| `allocator-rule` | The binding vouches for a rule of alignment or allocation that some build or allocator of the C does not keep: the maximum alignment, a zero-size resize, who may free whose storage. | It vouches only for what every configured allocator guarantees, and checks alignment at each constructor that copies. | Miri, UBSan, review |
| `adoption-condition` | An adoption takes ownership without stating when the C owns the storage: a sentinel pointer at zero capacity, one element listed twice, a buffer a pool still tracks. | The contract states the exact condition, and the Rust checks it before the owner can free or resize. | ASan, review |
| `count-wrap` | A reference count the C does not check wraps once safe Rust can leak clones, and the object is freed early. | A count that can wrap within a process's lifetime is checked before each increment, and the clone fails or aborts before it wraps. | Miri, review |
| `uninitialised-as-data` | Memory the C leaves unwritten is exposed as initialised Rust data, or the argument that the C writes it is false on some path. | The Rust views it as uninitialised until every path of the C is shown to write it; an export takes raw pointers and builds no reference over memory its caller may have left unwritten. | Miri, review |
| `aliasing-at-the-boundary` | A pointer the C keeps is derived from a borrow that a later reborrow ends, or Rust holds a reference over memory the C still writes or shares. | Every pointer the C keeps is derived from the original raw pointer, and a reference is handed out only over a span no C writer or co-owner reaches. | Miri, BSan, review |

### 1.3 Threads and callbacks

| id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `unsynchronised-global` | The C reads and writes global state, or initialises it lazily on first use, without synchronisation, so that safe calls on unrelated objects race. | The Rust initialises or serialises that state before any safe call reaches it. | TSan, review |
| `assumed-locking` | A `Send` or `Sync` proof assumes the C object's own locking covers every access, but a path skips the lock, reads after releasing it, or the object has none. | Thread safety is derived from every reader and writer of each field. | review |
| `callback-state` | A trampoline mishandles a panic, a refusal or a re-entry: a stored panic goes stale or a nested call drops it, a drop panics, the C goes on after a refusal, or the callback runs under a lock of the C. | A stored panic or stop belongs to one outermost call of the C, no drop panics, and a stop is promised only where the C can be stopped. | review |

A `# Safety` contract or a `// SAFETY:` proof that is wrong in a way no pattern above names
is still a finding: a contract is derived again from every safe method that relies on it
whenever one is added.

## 2. Findings

A finding of the `ub` or `contracts` objective names its pattern, or `new`, as
[`reviewing-reports`](../../verification/reviewing/reports/SKILL.md)'s Reports section describes. A
sanitizer's false positive is no finding and names none.

A finding of a known pattern means that its statement did not let the analysis recognise
the case, or that what prevents it was not enough. A finding that is `new` is a pattern the
catalogue lacks.

## 3. Evolution

The catalogue changes only from findings a reproducer proves, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes:

- a `new` finding is proposed as a pattern once it is stated without the target's names,
  with the finding as its evidence; one that can only be stated in the target's names is
  that campaign's lesson;
- a pattern whose findings recur has its statement or its prevention sharpened, from the
  findings that escaped it; and
- a pattern no campaign has met since it was written stays: its absence is what the
  catalogue is for.

What tells whether the catalogue works is the count of findings of known patterns, over
the modules integrated since a pattern was written, taken together: it falls against the
modules before, or the catalogue is not what prevents them. One module alone tells nothing,
since modules differ. The unsafe sites the reviews read, which the count would be taken
against, are not recorded yet. The count of `new` findings tells how much of what goes wrong
the catalogue does not hold yet.

name: ffibox
description: "The library the campaign's Rust holds C memory through, in both directions: owners, handles, lifecycle policies, status conventions, callbacks and exports. Read before writing any wrapper, owner, lifecycle strategy, callable type or export, when judging a crate for adoption, and when testing or reviewing one."
---

# ffibox

ffibox is the library a campaign's Rust expresses C's ownership and lifetime conventions
through, in both directions: memory C allocates, frees, copies, refcounts or locks, held
from Rust behind a safe API, and memory Rust owns that C holds, calls or reads. Its
primitives stand in for raw pointers and hand-written `Drop` impls wherever C aliases a
value; what C does not alias is plain Rust.

Its `README.md` is read in full before the first wrapper is written, and each section
below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. Which
primitive serves which C declaration, and how each is built, is those documents'. A
representation ffibox cannot express is hand-written, as its `docs/hand-written.md`
describes, with the same seam and safety-comment discipline. Its goals and non-goals,
`docs/goals.md`, are what a change to ffibox is judged against, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes.

What follows is how ffibox serves each stage: each section names the skill and section it
adds to, and states only what ffibox adds there.

## Planning

### Dependencies › Adopted crates

A candidate crate's soundness is read against the hazards `docs/goals.md`'s G9 lists,
each of which ffibox excludes from the campaign's own bindings: the crate qualifies where
its safe API excludes them too, by whatever means it uses.

## Binding workflow

### Binding workflow › Rust tree

The workspace depends on ffibox by path, on the checkout the host provides, which is on
the campaign's working branch of it, `ffibox = { path = "/crustify-rs/ffibox" }` in Crustify's image, so that
each run records its revision among its task's `revisions`. The path is the checkout's
canonical one, with no symbolic link on it, and a `[patch]` that redirects another source of
ffibox names the same: compile-fail snapshots normalize a path dependency only where the
compiler's paths match the dependency's canonical directory.
<!-- TODO: a released ffibox, as a versioned dependency, once `devel` reaches `main`.
Until then the path leaves the crate, against `bindgen`'s Layout section, and pins no
revision. -->

## Binding and porting

Binding reads `docs/ownership.md`, `docs/borrows.md`, `docs/patterns.md`,
`docs/vtables.md` and `docs/hand-written.md`; porting reads `docs/outbound.md` too.

### Binding types

A type that stays interoperable with C is bound through ffibox's primitives wherever they
apply, as `docs/ownership.md` and `docs/borrows.md` walk from its C declaration to them.

### Binding types › Safe layout

While a type keeps its C layout, `define_ctype!` mints `Foo`, `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>`,
and its owners are aliases of ffibox's owners over the policy that names its lifecycle
routines: `pub type FooBox = CBox<Foo, FooFree>;`, and `CArc<Foo, P>` for `FooArc`. A
value held inline that disposes its resources on drop is a `CVal<Foo, P>`.

### Binding symbols › Functions

A C routine's status convention becomes a `Result` through `status`, an object returned
through an out-parameter a return value through `from_c_out` or `from_raw_out`, and C's
iteration conventions iterators, as `docs/patterns.md` maps them.

### Binding symbols › Function pointers

A function pointer's callable type is a `CCallback`, where C holds it for a call or a
borrow, or a `CCallbackBox`, where C keeps it until it releases its context. Its Rust half
is a closure, a `CClosure` or a `CPayload`, which C reaches through its trampoline; its C
half is a C function with its context, a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, which Rust calls, built only
inside the crate through its `unsafe` constructor. A trampoline is the panic barrier,
`callback::barrier`, which also guards an export's body.
A struct of function pointers a library calls into, implemented by a Rust trait, is a
`CTable` whose slots `impl_cvtable!` mints, over the binding's own `unsafe impl CVtable`, as
`docs/vtables.md` describes; a table C implements is held as any other C object. A family of
hooks that carries no context is trampolines over `callback::barrier`, not a table.

### Binding symbols › Lifecycle strategies

Each lifecycle is held by the owner `docs/ownership.md` chooses for its shape, over the
policy that names its routines; a policy with state, such as an allocator context, is held
by `CBoxState`. A Rust value whose release C drives, such as a refcounted user payload, is
a `CPayload`, released through the routine it gives C.

### Porting › FFI boundary

An export gateway is built from the primitives `docs/outbound.md` chooses for what C does
with the Rust it reaches:

- the lifecycle routines C still calls on a ported type are `export_cnew!`,
  `export_cdrop!` and `export_cdupclone!` over the type's policy, which take and return
  its owners and handles;
- memory C frees comes from the allocator C frees it with: Rust's, `RustAlloc`, when C
  frees it through an exported release;
- a callback C passes an export is a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, and a value C keeps a
  `CPayload`; and
- the gateway's body runs in `callback::barrier`.

### Porting types › Structs

Until a ported struct's `port/layout`, its handles are ffibox's, as
[Binding types › Safe layout](#binding-types--safe-layout) describes; from it
on, `FooRef` and `FooMut` are aliases of native borrows. Its owners stay ffibox's until its
`port/memory`, or until its `port/layout` where that comes first, as below, their policy
calling its lifecycle routines, C's through their raw bindings until each is ported, then
the Rust ones. A `port/memory` before its `port/layout` keeps them ffibox's and changes their
policy to `RustAlloc` alone: `FooBox` becomes `CBox<Foo, RustAlloc>`, its handles unchanged,
until its `port/layout` makes it `Box<Foo>`, or `Pin<Box<Foo>>` while C keeps its address.

Between a struct's `port/layout` and its `port/memory`, its layout is native while C still
allocates or frees its storage, and ffibox's single-object owners, which hold only C-layout
types, cannot hold it. Where C releases it with its allocation family's free alone, and the
native type is not zero-sized and needs no drop (`size_of::<Foo>() != 0` and
`!core::mem::needs_drop::<Foo>()`, both asserted at compile time), and C does not keep its
address, `FooBox` is `Box<Foo, CAllocator<P>>` and a counted run of them `Vec<Foo,
CAllocator<P>>`, `P` the family's `Copy` policy with the alignment the family guarantees: an
existing `CLenAlloc` policy of the family, or one declared with `impl_clenalloc!`'s `align
=`. A box is built with `CAllocator::try_box`, which refuses an over-aligned type at compile
time and returns C's out-of-memory failure, and handed to C with
`Box::into_raw_with_allocator`; a run grows with `Vec::try_reserve`, keeping C's
out-of-memory failure, and is handed to C through `CVec::try_from` and `into_raw_parts`. A
pointer C hands back is adopted with `Box::from_raw_in`, under the conditions
`CBox::into_box`'s documentation lists, and a run with `Vec::from_raw_parts_in`, its length
as its capacity, under the allocator's fit rule. Its `port/memory` makes them `Box<Foo>` and
`Vec<Foo>`.
<!-- TODO: a native-layout struct, between its `port/layout` and its `port/memory`, that C
releases through a lifecycle routine of its own, that needs drop, whose address C keeps
(`Pin<Box<Foo, A>>` needs an allocator std does not accept yet) or that is reference-counted
(`Arc::new_in` is unstable) has no owner ffibox or std provides: it is hand-written until one
exists, or its `port/memory` is scheduled no later than its `port/layout`. -->

## Testing

### Testing › UB tests

The public seam interface ffibox exports on a type is meant to be exercised inside the
crate only, as an escape hatch for external consumers, so it gets no UB tests: a test of
it, for UB or functionality, is a unit test.

## Reviewing

Reviewing reads `docs/goals.md`.

### Revi

5	
6	# Generating safe bindings
7	
8	How a scheduled C item becomes a safe Rust binding.
9	A binding keeps the C implementation and puts a safe Rust API in front of it, shaped by the
10	item's analysis, as [`analysis`](../analysis/SKILL.md) describes. A type takes the type
11	route, for structs, unions, enums and typedefs, as [`binding-types`](types/SKILL.md)
12	describes; a symbol the symbol route, for functions, globals, function pointers, macros and
13	lifecycle strategies, as [`binding-symbols`](symbols/SKILL.md) describes.
14	
15	## 1. Safe boundary
16	
17	Any ABI or layout C still observes is preserved, and imported entities remain C-owned.
18	
19	Rust consumers use safe APIs. Raw operations are confined to:
20	
21	- wrapped-layout projection;
22	- wrapped FFI calls; and
23	- operations whose caller obligation cannot be represented in Rust types.
24	
25	They sit in their module's unsafe regions, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)'
26	Unsafe regions section lays them out, and a region's soundness rests on the region alone:
27	each item it exposes is sound for every input the rest of its module can give it, the
28	invariants its unsafe code relies on being held in the region's own private fields or
29	guaranteed by the library the bindings hold C memory through or the standard library, never by data the native code can build or
30	change. It exposes no field its unsafe code relies on, and no `unsafe fn` beyond the
31	public ones whose obligation no type expresses.
32	
33	The obligation of an `unsafe fn` that stores a value C keeps, such as a pointer a later
34	call follows, lasts as long as C holds it, in the object or in any copy C makes of it: until
35	a setter replaces it or a call clears it, the contract naming which, or else as long as its
36	holders live. It is never bounded by the calls that use the value, since safe code makes
37	those after the `unsafe` call has returned.
38	
39	A confirmed C defect, a behaviour that departs from the C's specification as
40	[`reviewing`](../../verification/reviewing/SKILL.md)'s `logic` objective orders it, is not
41	carried into the safe API. Where Rust can tell the defect's input before the call, the
42	binding refuses it, with the error the C gives an invalid input; where it cannot, it
43	composes the item from the routines its C calls, through their own bindings and in the
44	C's order, correcting the defect, and its anchor is `Replaces`, as a port's is, its alias
45	kept. A lifecycle primitive that is defective only on a failure path is composed so,
46	while its policy still calls the primitives that are not. Each divergence is documented
47	on the item, and kept by a unit test, as [`testing`](../../verification/testing/SKILL.md)'s
48	Equivalence tests section describes.
49	
50	A dependency on a module that runs later, cut from a cycle, is reached through the safe
51	wrappers a wrap batch adds before its consumer, never through raw bindings. A wrapper over
52	the items of a module that will be ported is written as that module's API: the names,
53	ownership and error types its port keeps, so that its consumers do not change when it
54	ports. Every unsafe block carries
55	the safety comment [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Unsafe code section specifies.
56	
57	An out-of-tree library's entity, such as libc's or libm's, is reached through the Rust
58	standard library wherever it provides it and the state the entity works on stays in Rust,
59	or crosses to C only as values the boundary converts: `errno` set from an `io::Error` by
60	an export gateway, a `struct stat` filled from an `fs::Metadata`. It is reached through the
61	library's bindings wherever that state is shared with C: a lock, a handle or an allocation
62	the remaining C uses too. `dependencies.json` recommends a route for each entity, which a
63	library's `decision` adopts or overrides; the first batch that needs the entity checks that
64	route against the code it translates, takes another the decision allows where it does not
65	hold, and reports which in its final message, as
66	[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)'s Confirmation section describes. An
67	entity needed through a wrapper that lacks it is reported, never reached through raw
68	bindings.

73	
74	# Binding types
75	
76	How a scheduled C type becomes a safe Rust binding: the type route, which follows
77	[`binding`](../SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section; the symbols it reaches are
78	[`binding-symbols`](../symbols/SKILL.md)'s. [`porting-types`](../../porting/types/SKILL.md)
79	starts from it.
80	
81	## 1. Surface
82	
83	A binding's surface is the fields and lifecycle primitives the public API publishes: in a
84	wrap batch that precedes its consumers, the fields those consumers access and the
85	type's lifecycle primitives, so that a type none of whose fields they access is bound
86	opaque.
87	Releasers, field disposers, cloners, constructors, casts and pointer-field semantics are
88	identified before a representation is chosen.
89	
90	## 2. Safe layout
91	
92	A type is bound as a safe layout over the raw type and its handles. The canonical wrapped
93	surface has three types, named as the conventions describe:
94	
95	| type | role |
96	|---|---|
97	| `Foo` | layout-compatible newtype named in every owner and handle, and held by value only in Rust-owned storage (a local, or embedded) |
98	| `FooRef<'a>` | copyable shared borrowed handle with getters |
99	| `FooMut<'a>` | exclusive borrowed handle with setters, and shared and exclusive reborrows |
100	
101	Its owners, which [Lifecycle](#3-lifecycle) describes, are named `FooBox` and `FooArc`, as
102	the conventions name them too. These names are what consumers use, whatever they name: here
103	pointer wrappers and owners over C's allocator, which a port changes, stage by stage, into
104	native borrows and owners, as [`porting-types`](../../porting/types/SKILL.md)'s Structs section describes,
105	without changing its consumers. A consumer relies only on what every form they may take
106	offers: their methods, their reborrows (`as_ref`, `as_mut`) and the dereferences the
107	native forms offer, which the pointer wrappers mirror. What one form offers beyond that,
108	such as an owner's raw access, is no part of the safe API.
109	
110	No Rust reference to the wrapped C object is ever formed. Borrowed handles contain
111	pointers and carry lifetimes; references to handles cover Rust-owned handle storage only.
112	Layout access starts from `FooRef::as_ptr()` or `FooMut::as_mut_ptr()`, in small justified
113	unsafe blocks.
114	
115	A synthetic type generator is bound as:
116	
117	- a generic wrapper for a homogeneous family converging on the generator;
118	- an alias of a dominant concrete instance to the generator with its element wrapper; and
119	- specializations only for behaviour that differs from the generic surface.
120	
121	## 3. Lifecycle
122	
123	Every ownership variant the analysis supports has a representation.
124	
125	Owners never dereference to `Foo`; they hand out handles. A sole owner, or a `Foo` value,
126	produces `FooRef` and `FooMut` through `as_ref()` and `as_mut()`. A shared owner without a
127	lock produces `FooRef` directly, and `FooMut` only when it can prove its reference is the
128	only one, or after copying the object. A shared owner whose object carries its own lock
129	produces both through read and write guards, which hold the lock while the handle lives.
130	
131	Lifecycle and clone
132	strategies are stateless, layout-compatible and statically selected when the state is
133	recoverable from the object; runtime state is carried only when construction, destruction
134	or cloning needs external data.
135	
136	A type's constructor and init routines are bound with its lifecycle policy, so that where
137	possible it is exported as a safe function returning the fully-formed object. Every type an
138	argument names is wrapped before it, since a wrap brings in its signature's types.
139	
140	C lifecycle primitives are kept while C can allocate or free the storage.
141	
142	A type whose address C keeps beyond the call that receives it, to read it, call back with it
143	or free it, as the analysis establishes, is never moved while C keeps it: a value of it
144	held by value is never handed to C to keep, and an owner that could move it out is
145	pinned.
146	
147	Promoting construction-phase storage into an owner is unsafe, so it is encapsulated in the
148	type's safe constructor: consumers of the public API never call `assume_init` in their own
149	unsafe blocks.
150	
151	Lifecycle routines are also scheduled as free symbols, although the type route emits them
152	as it binds their types; the symbol route, [`binding-symbols`](../symbols/SKILL.md)'s,
153	skips those a type batch already emitted.
154	
155	## 4. Field accessors
156	
157	Each accessor follows from the ownership, mutability, nullability, cardinality and lifetime
158	findings, and every pointer-derived result is tied to the state that keeps it alive.
159	
160	Getters that read `Foo`'s fields are methods in `impl FooRef` blocks taking `&self`, and
161	setters that write them are methods in `impl FooMut` blocks taking `&mut self`. A field is
162	read through the shared handle's pointer and written through the mutable handle's pointer,
163	projected with `addr_of!`, `addr_of_mut!`, `&raw const` or `&raw mut`, never with
164	`&(*p).field` or `&mut (*p).field`.
165	
166	Each kind of field is expressed as follows:
167	
168	- An owned-reference field has a replacement setter that drops the old owner, an owning
169	  getter that leaves the field valid, and a shared borrowed getter.
170	- A by-value wrapped field has a shared or mutable handle over the projected place.
171	- A stored borrow without an expressible lifetime has an unsafe setter whose caller
172	  contract carries the referent-lifetime obligation.
173	- Statically known owned and borrowed cases have distinct wrapper forms, with a shared
174	  trait where useful.
175	- A runtime ownership flag has separately checked owned and borrowed operations.
176	- A union field and its discriminator are one accessor of a tagged Rust enum, as
177	  [Unions](#5-unions) describes.
178	- Scalar and array variants have separate typed forms.
179	- A type-erased field takes a generic element type when it is known, and the discovered
180	  untyped lifetime strategy otherwise. One whose pointee's type a sibling field selects,
181	  as a kind tag does, is presented as a union is: one tagged enum over the tag and the
182	  pointer, each variant holding its type's safe form, read from both and written together,
183	  so that no setter writes the tag alone.
184	- `Send` and `Sync` are implemented only with a specific synchronization or immutability
185	  proof.
186	
187	Translated dependent types and function pointers are used through their safe wrappers,
188	and strings, arrays and erased owners through real release strategies.
189	
190	An inline function-pointer helper without an ownership-compatible wrapper gets one,
191	emitted with the type.
192	
193	## 5. Unions
194	
195	A union is not bound as a type of its own: the types its members hold are bound, and the
196	union is presented where it is used, a field accessor or a function's signature, as a
197	tagged Rust enum, with a variant for each member, each over its member's safe type. One
198	tagged enum stands in for the union at every use. Its tag is the discriminator the
199	analysis establishes as selecting the active member: a sibling field, a parameter, or a
200	predicate over sibling fields, such as a length that is zero only while an inline member
201	is active. Reading the union evaluates the discriminator to choose the variant, and
202	writing it writes both.
203	
204	A union whose active member nothing beside it selects, its tag held by what refers to it,
205	such as the sign of the index that reaches it, is presented by an `unsafe` accessor for
206	each member, whose caller contract states which member must be active.
207	
208	## 6. Enums
209	
210	An enum is bound to a safe Rust type over the constants bindgen generates for it:
211	
212	- a closed enum is a Rust enum, with a variant for each of its constants;
213	- an enum whose constants C combines as flags is a `#[repr(transparent)]` newtype over its
214	  integer type, with an associated constant for each of its constants and the bitwise
215	  operators, since a combination is no variant; and
216	- an enum without a name has no type to bind: its constants become constants of its
217	  integer type.
218	
219	Beneath a closed enum's safe type sits its integer form, the interop layer C needs: a
220	`#[repr]` over the enum's integer type, as bindgen gives it, each constant's value its
221	variant's discriminant, and the conversions through which its values cross the boundary
222	as that integer. A value from C is converted fallibly where it enters Rust, since C may
223	pass one the enum does not name, which a Rust enum may not hold: such a value takes the
224	path the C gives an invalid value, or an error of the safe API where it gives none. A
225	binding keeps the integer form for good, since C implements what produces and consumes
226	the enum's values.
227	
228	## 7. Typedefs
229	
230	A typedef of its own, one that names no struct, union, enum or function pointer, gives
231	another name to a type that has a Rust form already: a primitive, an array, a pointer, or a
232	type another link unit or an out-of-tree library's wrapper owns. It is bound under its own
233	name to the Rust form the analysis shapes from its uses: an alias of the type it names where
234	they give it no meaning that type lacks, and a type of its own where they do, an invariant,
235	an ownership or a type erasure that an alias would flatten. Its raw form is no part of the
236	safe API, as [`binding`](../SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section describes, and it has no interop layer of
237	its own: its values cross the boundary as those of the type it names do.
238	---
239	name: soundness
240	description: "The patterns by which safe Rust over C has reached undefined behaviour in Crustify's campaigns, each with what prevents it and which check catches it, and how the catalogue grows from proven findings. Read before analysing, binding or porting any item, before writing its UB tests, and when reviewing for UB or contracts."
241	---
242	
243	# Soundness patterns
244	
245	The ways a binding or a port of C has let safe Rust reach undefined behaviour, or met a
246	memory-safety defect of the C that it had to keep out of its safe API. Every pattern here
247	has a proven finding of a campaign behind it: the catalogue records what went wrong, not
248	what could. An item's analysis asks of each pattern whether the item can meet it, and a
249	review for UB or contracts reads the item against the same list, so that a defect one
250	module met is not met again in the next.
251	
252	## 1. Patterns
253	
254	Each pattern has an id, which a finding's report names. What prevents a pattern is stated
255	as what the Rust does; [`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md) and [`porting`](../porting/SKILL.md)
256	give the routes that do it.
257	
258	### 1.1 Values the C trusts
259	
260	| id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by |
261	|---|---|---|---|
262	| `unchecked-arithmetic` | The C computes with a value a safe caller controls and does not check it: a signed overflow, a shift, a size that wraps with its header, a zero divisor. | The Rust checks the value's range before the call, sizes past `isize::MAX` included, and refuses what the C would compute wrongly. | UBSan, review |
263	| `diverging-precheck` | A check in Rust repeats the C's parsing or evaluation and differs from what the C then computes. | The Rust validates the exact value the C will use, or computes the result itself and hands the C only that. | UBSan |
264	| `degenerate-input` | The C reads out of bounds on an input its own validation accepts, such as an empty string beside others or a null pointer for a string. | Every wrapper that can route the input to that reader refuses or normalises it, the indirect routes included. | ASan |
265	| `variant-mismatch` | A tagged, variable-size value of another variant than its container expects is passed on, and the C sizes its buffers by the container's. | The Rust compares the value's variant with the container's before any call that looks it up or formats it. | ASan |
266	
267	### 1.2 Memory and ownership
268	
269	| id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by |
270	|---|---|---|---|
271	| `size-known-to-c` | Only the C knows an object's true size or layout: an opaque type, a pointer a tag types, a base struct its callbacks read past, an array sized by a count. Rust builds it too small or types it wrongly. | Such an object is allocated through the C alone, a tagged pointer is typed only where its tag is vouched for, and an object whose callbacks read more than Rust built is refused. | ASan, review |
272	| `hidden-dependency` | A handle, a lent pointer or a callback outlives something it depends on without showing it: a parent it points back to, a global the program may close, lent memory the C copied into a second slot. | The handle's lifetime is tied to that owner, or it keeps the owner alive; a pointer the C stores is bounded by its longest-lived reader. | ASan, Miri, review |
273	| `failure-leaves-state` | A failure path of the C, most often a failed allocation, leaves an object uninitialised, freed, wrongly sized or half written and still returns, sometimes reporting success. | The Rust trusts nothing the C leaves after a failure: it validates outputs again, does not reuse the object, and composes the operation itself where the C's error path is unsafe. | ASan, UBSan, review |
274	| `allocator-rule` | The binding vouches for a rule of alignment or allocation that some build or allocator of the C does not keep: the maximum alignment, a zero-size resize, who may free whose storage. | It vouches only for what every configured allocator guarantees, and checks alignment at each constructor that copies. | Miri, UBSan, review |
275	| `adoption-condition` | An adoption takes ownership without stating when the C owns the storage: a sentinel pointer at zero capacity, one element listed twice, a buffer a pool still tracks. | The contract states the exact condition, and the Rust checks it before the owner can free or resize. | ASan, review |
276	| `count-wrap` | A reference count the C does not check wraps once safe Rust can leak clones, and the object is freed early. | A count that can wrap within a process's lifetime is checked before each increment, and the clone fails or aborts before it wraps. | Miri, review |
277	| `uninitialised-as-data` | Memory the C leaves unwritten is exposed as initialised Rust data, or the argument that the C writes it is false on some path. | The Rust views it as uninitialised until every path of the C is shown to write it; an export takes raw pointers and builds no reference over memory its caller may have left unwritten. | Miri, review |
278	| `aliasing-at-the-boundary` | A pointer the C keeps is derived from a borrow that a later reborrow ends, or Rust holds a reference over memory the C still writes or shares. | Every pointer the C keeps is derived from the original raw pointer, and a reference is handed out only over a span no C writer or co-owner reaches. | Miri, BSan, review |
279	
280	### 1.3 Threads and callbacks
281	
282	| id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by |
283	|---|---|---|---|
284	| `unsynchronised-global` | The C reads and writes global state, or initialises it lazily on first use, without synchronisation, so that safe calls on unrelated objects race. | The Rust initialises or serialises that state before any safe call reaches it. | TSan, review |
285	| `assumed-locking` | A `Send` or `Sync` proof assumes the C object's own locking covers every access, but a path skips the lock, reads after releasing it, or the object has none. | Thread safety is derived from every reader and writer of each field. | review |
286	| `callback-state` | A trampoline mishandles a panic, a refusal or a re-entry: a stored panic goes stale or a nested call drops it, a drop panics, the C goes on after a refusal, or the callback runs under a lock of the C. | A stored panic or stop belongs to one outermost call of the C, no drop panics, and a stop is promised only where the C can be stopped. | review |
287	
288	A `# Safety` contract or a `// SAFETY:` proof that is wrong in a way no pattern above names
289	is still a finding: a contract is derived again from every safe method that relies on it
290	whenever one is added.
291	
292	## 2. Findings
293	
294	A finding of the `ub` or `contracts` objective names its pattern, or `new`, as
295	[`reviewing-reports`](../../verification/reviewing/reports/SKILL.md)'s Reports section describes. A
296	sanitizer's false positive is no finding and names none.
297	
298	A finding of a known pattern means that its statement did not let the analysis recognise
299	the case, or that what prevents it was not enough. A finding that is `new` is a pattern the
300	catalogue lacks.
301	
302	## 3. Evolution
303	
304	The catalogue changes only from findings a reproducer proves, as
305	[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes:
306	
307	- a `new` finding is proposed as a pattern once it is stated without the target's names,
308	  with the finding as its evidence; one that can only be stated in the target's names is
309	  that campaign's lesson;
310	- a pattern whose findings recur has its statement or its prevention sharpened, from the
311	  findings that escaped it; and
312	- a pattern no campaign has met since it was written stays: its absence is what the
313	  catalogue is for.
314	
315	What tells whether the catalogue works is the count of findings of known patterns, over
316	the modules integrated since a pattern was written, taken together: it falls against the
317	modules before, or the catalogue is not what prevents them. One module alone tells nothing,
318	since modules differ. The unsafe sites the reviews read, which the count would be taken
319	against, are not recorded yet. The count of `new` findings tells how much of what goes wrong
320	the catalogue does not hold yet.
321	---
322	name: ffibox
323	description: "The library the campaign's Rust holds C memory through, in both directions: owners, handles, lifecycle policies, status conventions, callbacks and exports. Read before writing any wrapper, owner, lifecycle strategy, callable type or export, when judging a crate for adoption, and when testing or reviewing one."
324	---
325	
326	# ffibox
327	
328	ffibox is the library a campaign's Rust expresses C's ownership and lifetime conventions
329	through, in both directions: memory C allocates, frees, copies, refcounts or locks, held
330	from Rust behind a safe API, and memory Rust owns that C holds, calls or reads. Its
331	primitives stand in for raw pointers and hand-written `Drop` impls wherever C aliases a
332	value; what C does not alias is plain Rust.
333	
334	Its `README.md` is read in full before the first wrapper is written, and each section
335	below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. Which
336	primitive serves which C declaration, and how each is built, is those documents'. A
337	representation ffibox cannot express is hand-written, as its `docs/hand-written.md`
338	describes, with the same seam and safety-comment discipline. Its goals and non-goals,
339	`docs/goals.md`, are what a change to ffibox is judged against, as
340	[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes.
341	
342	What follows is how ffibox serves each stage: each section names the skill and section it
343	adds to, and states only what ffibox adds there.
344	
345	## Planning
346	
347	### Dependencies › Adopted crates
348	
349	A candidate crate's soundness is read against the hazards `docs/goals.md`'s G9 lists,
350	each of which ffibox excludes from the campaign's own bindings: the crate qualifies where
351	its safe API excludes them too, by whatever means it uses.
352	
353	## Binding workflow
354	
355	### Binding workflow › Rust tree
356	
357	The workspace depends on ffibox by path, on the checkout the host provides, which is on
358	the campaign's working branch of it, `ffibox = { path = "/crustify-rs/ffibox" }` in Crustify's image, so that
359	each run records its revision among its task's `revisions`. The path is the checkout's
360	canonical one, with no symbolic link on it, and a `[patch]` that redirects another source of
361	ffibox names the same: compile-fail snapshots normalize a path dependency only where the
362	compiler's paths match the dependency's canonical directory.
363	<!-- TODO: a released ffibox, as a versioned dependency, once `devel` reaches `main`.
364	Until then the path leaves the crate, against `bindgen`'s Layout section, and pins no
365	revision. -->
366	
367	## Binding and porting
368	
369	Binding reads `docs/ownership.md`, `docs/borrows.md`, `docs/patterns.md`,
370	`docs/vtables.md` and `docs/hand-written.md`; porting reads `docs/outbound.md` too.
371	
372	### Binding types
373	
374	A type that stays interoperable with C is bound through ffibox's primitives wherever they
375	apply, as `docs/ownership.md` and `docs/borrows.md` walk from its C declaration to them.
376	
377	### Binding types › Safe layout
378	
379	While a type keeps its C layout, `define_ctype!` mints `Foo`, `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>`,
380	and its owners are aliases of ffibox's owners over the policy that names its lifecycle
381	routines: `pub type FooBox = CBox<Foo, FooFree>;`, and `CArc<Foo, P>` for `FooArc`. A
382	value held inline that disposes its resources on drop is a `CVal<Foo, P>`.
383	
384	### Binding symbols › Functions
385	
386	A C routine's status convention becomes a `Result` through `status`, an object returned
387	through an out-parameter a return value through `from_c_out` or `from_raw_out`, and C's
388	iteration conventions iterators, as `docs/patterns.md` maps them.
389	
390	### Binding symbols › Function pointers
391	
392	A function pointer's callable type is a `CCallback`, where C holds it for a call or a
393	borrow, or a `CCallbackBox`, where C keeps it until it releases its context. Its Rust half
394	is a closure, a `CClosure` or a `CPayload`, which C reaches through its trampoline; its C
395	half is a C function with its context, a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, which Rust calls, built only
396	inside the crate through its `unsafe` constructor. A trampoline is the panic barrier,
397	`callback::barrier`, which also guards an export's body.
398	A struct of function pointers a library calls into, implemented by a Rust trait, is a
399	`CTable` whose slots `impl_cvtable!` mints, over the binding's own `unsafe impl CVtable`, as
400	`docs/vtables.md` describes; a table C implements is held as any other C object. A family of
401	hooks that carries no context is trampolines over `callback::barrier`, not a table.
402	
403	### Binding symbols › Lifecycle strategies
404	
405	Each lifecycle is held by the owner `docs/ownership.md` chooses for its shape, over the
406	policy that names its routines; a policy with state, such as an allocator context, is held
407	by `CBoxState`. A Rust value whose release C drives, such as a refcounted user payload, is
408	a `CPayload`, released through the routine it gives C.
409	
410	### Porting › FFI boundary
411	
412	An export gateway is built from the primitives `docs/outbound.md` chooses for what C does
413	with the Rust it reaches:
414	
415	- the lifecycle routines C still calls on a ported type are `export_cnew!`,
416	  `export_cdrop!` and `export_cdupclone!` over the type's policy, which take and return
417	  its owners and handles;
418	- memory C frees comes from the allocator C frees it with: Rust's, `RustAlloc`, when C
419	  frees it through an exported release;
420	- a callback C passes an export is a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, and a value C keeps a
421	  `CPayload`; and
422	- the gateway's body runs in `callback::barrier`.
423	
424	### Porting types › Structs
425	
426	Until a ported struct's `port/layout`, its handles are ffibox's, as
427	[Binding types › Safe layout](#binding-types--safe-layout) describes; from it
428	on, `FooRef` and `FooMut` are aliases of native borrows. Its owners stay ffibox's until its
429	`port/memory`, or until its `port/layout` where that comes first, as below, their policy
430	calling its lifecycle routines, C's through their raw bindings until each is ported, then
431	the Rust ones. A `port/memory` before its `port/layout` keeps them ffibox's and changes their
432	policy to `RustAlloc` alone: `FooBox` becomes `CBox<Foo, RustAlloc>`, its handles unchanged,
433	until its `port/layout` makes it `Box<Foo>`, or `Pin<Box<Foo>>` while C keeps its address.
434	
435	Between a struct's `port/layout` and its `port/memory`, its layout is native while C still
436	allocates or frees its storage, and ffibox's single-object owners, which hold only C-layout
437	types, cannot hold it. Where C releases it with its allocation family's free alone, and the
438	native type is not zero-sized and needs no drop (`size_of::<Foo>() != 0` and
439	`!core::mem::needs_drop::<Foo>()`, both asserted at compile time), and C does not keep its
440	address, `FooBox` is `Box<Foo, CAllocator<P>>` and a counted run of them `Vec<Foo,
441	CAllocator<P>>`, `P` the family's `Copy` policy with the alignment the family guarantees: an
442	existing `CLenAlloc` policy of the family, or one declared with `impl_clenalloc!`'s `align
443	=`. A box is built with `CAllocator::try_box`, which refuses an over-aligned type at compile
444	time and returns C's out-of-memory failure, and handed to C with
445	`Box::into_raw_with_allocator`; a run grows with `Vec::try_reserve`, keeping C's
446	out-of-memory failure, and is handed to C through `CVec::try_from` and `into_raw_parts`. A
447	pointer C hands back is adopted with `Box::from_raw_in`, under the conditions
448	`CBox::into_box`'s documentation lists, and a run with `Vec::from_raw_parts_in`, its length
449	as its capacity, under the allocator's fit rule. Its `port/memory` makes them `Box<Foo>` and
450	`Vec<Foo>`.
451	<!-- TODO: a native-layout struct, between its `port/layout` and its `port/memory`, that C
452	releases through a lifecycle routine of its own, that needs drop, whose address C keeps
453	(`Pin<Box<Foo, A>>` needs an allocator std does not accept yet) or that is reference-counted
454	(`Arc::new_in` is unstable) has no owner ffibox or std provides: it is hand-written until one
455	exists, or its `port/memory` is scheduled no later than its `port/layout`. -->
456	
457	## Testing
458	
459	### Testing › UB tests
460	
461	The public seam interface ffibox exports on a type is meant to be exercised inside the
462	crate only, as an escape hatch for external consumers, so it gets no UB tests: a test of
463	it, for UB or functionality, is a unit test.
464	
465	## Reviewing
466	
467	Reviewing reads `docs/goals.md`.
468	
469	### Reviewing › Objectives
470	
471	A workset's use of ffibox's primitives is reviewed against ffibox's documentation, and its
472	hand-written representations against the contract ffibox would have enforced. Under `ub`,
473	the hazards `docs/goals.md`'s G9 lists are the checklist: each is excluded by the
474	primitive or the producer's contract it names, or is a finding.
475	
476	### Reviewing-reports › Reports
477	
478	A soundness or ergonomics gap in ffibox itself, in its safe primitives or its unsafe FFI
479	seams, is a defect in a tool: a proposal, as any tool defect is.
480

---
name: binding
description: "How a scheduled C item becomes a safe Rust binding: the safe boundary every binding keeps, and the routes binding-types and binding-symbols give types and symbols. Read before binding any item, and when reviewing bindings."
---

# Generating safe bindings

How a scheduled C item becomes a safe Rust binding.
A binding keeps the C implementation and puts a safe Rust API in front of it, shaped by the
item's analysis, as [`analysis`](../analysis/SKILL.md) describes. A type takes the type
route, for structs, unions, enums and typedefs, as [`binding-types`](types/SKILL.md)
describes; a symbol the symbol route, for functions, globals, function pointers, macros and
lifecycle strategies, as [`binding-symbols`](symbols/SKILL.md) describes.

## 1. Safe boundary

Any ABI or layout C still observes is preserved, and imported entities remain C-owned.

Rust consumers use safe APIs. Raw operations are confined to:

- wrapped-layout projection;
- wrapped FFI calls; and
- operations whose caller obligation cannot be represented in Rust types.

They sit in their module's unsafe regions, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)'
Unsafe regions section lays them out, and a region's soundness rests on the region alone:
each item it exposes is sound for every input the rest of its module can give it, the
invariants its unsafe code relies on being held in the region's own private fields or
guaranteed by the library the bindings hold C memory through or the standard library, never by data the native code can build or
change. It exposes no field its unsafe code relies on, and no `unsafe fn` beyond the
public ones whose obligation no type expresses.

The obligation of an `unsafe fn` that stores a value C keeps, such as a pointer a later
call follows, lasts as long as C holds it, in the object or in any copy C makes of it: until
a setter replaces it or a call clears it, the contract naming which, or else as long as its
holders live. It is never bounded by the calls that use the value, since safe code makes
those after the `unsafe` call has returned.

A confirmed C defect, a behaviour that departs from the C's specification as
[`reviewing`](../../verification/reviewing/SKILL.md)'s `logic` objective orders it, is not
carried into the safe API. Where Rust can tell the defect's input before the call, the
binding refuses it, with the error the C gives an invalid input; where it cannot, it
composes the item from the routines its C calls, through their own bindings and in the
C's order, correcting the defect, and its anchor is `Replaces`, as a port's is, its alias
kept. A lifecycle primitive that is defective only on a failure path is composed so,
while its policy still calls the primitives that are not. Each divergence is documented
on the item, and kept by a unit test, as [`testing`](../../verification/testing/SKILL.md)'s
Equivalence tests section describes.

A dependency on a module that runs later, cut from a cycle, is reached through the safe
wrappers a wrap batch adds before its consumer, never through raw bindings. A wrapper over
the items of a module that will be ported is written as that module's API: the names,
ownership and error types its port keeps, so that its consumers do not change when it
ports. Every unsafe block carries
the safety comment [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Unsafe code section specifies.

An out-of-tree library's entity, such as libc's or libm's, is reached through the Rust
standard library wherever it provides it and the state the entity works on stays in Rust,
or crosses to C only as values the boundary converts: `errno` set from an `io::Error` by
an export gateway, a `struct stat` filled from an `fs::Metadata`. It is reached through the
library's bindings wherever that state is shared with C: a lock, a handle or an allocation
the remaining C uses too. `dependencies.json` recommends a route for each entity, which a
library's `decision` adopts or overrides; the first batch that needs the entity checks that
route against the code it translates, takes another the decision allows where it does not
hold, and reports which in its final message, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)'s Confirmation section describes. An
entity needed through a wrapper that lacks it is reported, never reached through raw
bindings.

name: binding-types
description: "How a scheduled C type becomes a safe Rust binding, binding's type route: its surface, safe layout, lifecycle and field accessors, unions as tagged enums, enums and typedefs. Read before binding any type, and when reviewing bindings."
---

# Binding types

How a scheduled C type becomes a safe Rust binding: the type route, which follows
[`binding`](../SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section; the symbols it reaches are
[`binding-symbols`](../symbols/SKILL.md)'s. [`porting-types`](../../porting/types/SKILL.md)
starts from it.

## 1. Surface

A binding's surface is the fields and lifecycle primitives the public API publishes: in a
wrap batch that precedes its consumers, the fields those consumers access and the
type's lifecycle primitives, so that a type none of whose fields they access is bound
opaque.
Releasers, field disposers, cloners, constructors, casts and pointer-field semantics are
identified before a representation is chosen.

## 2. Safe layout

A type is bound as a safe layout over the raw type and its handles. The canonical wrapped
surface has three types, named as the conventions describe:

| type | role |
|---|---|
| `Foo` | layout-compatible newtype named in every owner and handle, and held by value only in Rust-owned storage (a local, or embedded) |
| `FooRef<'a>` | copyable shared borrowed handle with getters |
| `FooMut<'a>` | exclusive borrowed handle with setters, and shared and exclusive reborrows |

Its owners, which [Lifecycle](#3-lifecycle) describes, are named `FooBox` and `FooArc`, as
the conventions name them too. These names are what consumers use, whatever they name: here
pointer wrappers and owners over C's allocator, which a port changes, stage by stage, into
native borrows and owners, as [`porting-types`](../../porting/types/SKILL.md)'s Structs section describes,
without changing its consumers. A consumer relies only on what every form they may take
offers: their methods, their reborrows (`as_ref`, `as_mut`) and the dereferences the
native forms offer, which the pointer wrappers mirror. What one form offers beyond that,
such as an owner's raw access, is no part of the safe API.

No Rust reference to the wrapped C object is ever formed. Borrowed handles contain
pointers and carry lifetimes; references to handles cover Rust-owned handle storage only.
Layout access starts from `FooRef::as_ptr()` or `FooMut::as_mut_ptr()`, in small justified
unsafe blocks.

A synthetic type generator is bound as:

- a generic wrapper for a homogeneous family converging on the generator;
- an alias of a dominant concrete instance to the generator with its element wrapper; and
- specializations only for behaviour that differs from the generic surface.

## 3. Lifecycle

Every ownership variant the analysis supports has a representation.

Owners never dereference to `Foo`; they hand out handles. A sole owner, or a `Foo` value,
produces `FooRef` and `FooMut` through `as_ref()` and `as_mut()`. A shared owner without a
lock produces `FooRef` directly, and `FooMut` only when it can prove its reference is the
only one, or after copying the object. A shared owner whose object carries its own lock
produces both through read and write guards, which hold the lock while the handle lives.

Lifecycle and clone
strategies are stateless, layout-compatible and statically selected when the state is
recoverable from the object; runtime state is carried only when construction, destruction
or cloning needs external data.

A type's constructor and init routines are bound with its lifecycle policy, so that where
possible it is exported as a safe function returning the fully-formed object. Every type an
argument names is wrapped before it, since a wrap brings in its signature's types.

C lifecycle primitives are kept while C can allocate or free the storage.

A type whose address C keeps beyond the call that receives it, to read it, call back with it
or free it, as the analysis establishes, is never moved while C keeps it: a value of it
held by value is never handed to C to keep, and an owner that could move it out is
pinned.

Promoting construction-phase storage into an owner is unsafe, so it is encapsulated in the
type's safe constructor: consumers of the public API never call `assume_init` in their own
unsafe blocks.

Lifecycle routines are also scheduled as free symbols, although the type route emits them
as it binds their types; the symbol route, [`binding-symbols`](../symbols/SKILL.md)'s,
skips those a type batch already emitted.

## 4. Field accessors

Each accessor follows from the ownership, mutability, nullability, cardinality and lifetime
findings, and every pointer-derived result is tied to the state that keeps it alive.

Getters that read `Foo`'s fields are methods in `impl FooRef` blocks taking `&self`, and
setters that write them are methods in `impl FooMut` blocks taking `&mut self`. A field is
read through the shared handle's pointer and written through the mutable handle's pointer,
projected with `addr_of!`, `addr_of_mut!`, `&raw const` or `&raw mut`, never with
`&(*p).field` or `&mut (*p).field`.

Each kind of field is expressed as follows:

- An owned-reference field has a replacement setter that drops the old owner, an owning
  getter that leaves the field valid, and a shared borrowed getter.
- A by-value wrapped field has a shared or mutable handle over the projected place.
- A stored borrow without an expressible lifetime has an unsafe setter whose caller
  contract carries the referent-lifetime obligation.
- Statically known owned and borrowed cases have distinct wrapper forms, with a shared
  trait where useful.
- A runtime ownership flag has separately checked owned and borrowed operations.
- A union field and its discriminator are one accessor of a tagged Rust enum, as
  [Unions](#5-unions) describes.
- Scalar and array variants have separate typed forms.
- A type-erased field takes a generic element type when it is known, and the discovered
  untyped lifetime strategy otherwise. One whose pointee's type a sibling field selects,
  as a kind tag does, is presented as a union is: one tagged enum over the tag and the
  pointer, each variant holding its type's safe form, read from both and written together,
  so that no setter writes the tag alone.
- `Send` and `Sync` are implemented only with a specific synchronization or immutability
  proof.

Translated dependent types and function pointers are used through their safe wrappers,
and strings, arrays and erased owners through real release strategies.

An inline function-pointer helper without an ownership-compatible wrapper gets one,
emitted with the type.

## 5. Unions

A union is not bound as a type of its own: the types its members hold are bound, and the
union is presented where it is used, a field accessor or a function's signature, as a
tagged Rust enum, with a variant for each member, each over its member's safe type. One
tagged enum stands in for the union at every use. Its tag is the discriminator the
analysis establishes as selecting the active member: a sibling field, a parameter, or a
predicate over sibling fields, such as a length that is zero only while an inline member
is active. Reading the union evaluates the discriminator to choose the variant, and
writing it writes both.

A union whose active member nothing beside it selects, its tag held by what refers to it,
such as the sign of the index that reaches it, is presented by an `unsafe` accessor for
each member, whose caller contract states which member must be active.

## 6. Enums

An enum is bound to a safe Rust type over the constants bindgen generates for it:

- a closed enum is a Rust enum, with a variant for each of its constants;
- an enum whose constants C combines as flags is a `#[repr(transparent)]` newtype over its
  integer type, with an associated constant for each of its constants and the bitwise
  operators, since a combination is no variant; and
- an enum without a name has no type to bind: its constants become constants of its
  integer type.

Beneath a closed enum's safe type sits its integer form, the interop layer C needs: a
`#[repr]` over the enum's integer type, as bindgen gives it, each constant's value its
variant's discriminant, and the conversions through which its values cross the boundary
as that integer. A value from C is converted fallibly where it enters Rust, since C may
pass one the enum does not name, which a Rust enum may not hold: such a value takes the
path the C gives an invalid value, or an error of the safe API where it gives none. A
binding keeps the integer form for good, since C implements what produces and consumes
the enum's values.

## 7. Typedefs

A typedef of its own, one that names no struct, union, enum or function pointer, gives
another name to a type that has a Rust form already: a primitive, an array, a pointer, or a
type another link unit or an out-of-tree library's wrapper owns. It is bound under its own
name to the Rust form the analysis shapes from its uses: an alias of the type it names where
they give it no meaning that type lacks, and a type of its own where they do, an invariant,
an ownership or a type erasure that an alias would flatten. Its raw form is no part of the
safe API, as [`binding`](../SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section describes, and it has no interop layer of
its own: its values cross the boundary as those of the type it names do.

name: soundness
description: "The patterns by which safe Rust over C has reached undefined behaviour in Crustify's campaigns, each with what prevents it and which check catches it, and how the catalogue grows from proven findings. Read before analysing, binding or porting any item, before writing its UB tests, and when reviewing for UB or contracts."

# Soundness patterns

The ways a binding or a port of C has let safe Rust reach undefined behaviour, or met a
memory-safety defect of the C that it had to keep out of its safe API. Every pattern here
has a proven finding of a campaign behind it: the catalogue records what went wrong, not
what could. An item's analysis asks of each pattern whether the item can meet it, and a
review for UB or contracts reads the item against the same list, so that a defect one
module met is not met again in the next.

## 1. Patterns

Each pattern has an id, which a finding's report names. What prevents a pattern is stated
as what the Rust does; [`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md) and [`porting`](../porting/SKILL.md)
give the routes that do it.

### 1.1 Values the C trusts

| id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `unchecked-arithmetic` | The C computes with a value a safe caller controls and does not check it: a signed overflow, a shift, a size that wraps with its header, a zero divisor. | The Rust checks the value's range before the call, sizes past `isize::MAX` included, and refuses what the C would compute wrongly. | UBSan, review |
| `diverging-precheck` | A check in Rust repeats the C's parsing or evaluation and differs from what the C then computes. | The Rust validates the exact value the C will use, or computes the result itself and hands the C only that. | UBSan |
| `degenerate-input` | The C reads out of bounds on an input its own validation accepts, such as an empty string beside others or a null pointer for a string. | Every wrapper that can route the input to that reader refuses or normalises it, the indirect routes included. | ASan |
| `variant-mismatch` | A tagged, variable-size value of another variant than its container expects is passed on, and the C sizes its buffers by the container's. | The Rust compares the value's variant with the container's before any call that looks it up or formats it. | ASan |

### 1.2 Memory and ownership

| id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `size-known-to-c` | Only the C knows an object's true size or layout: an opaque type, a pointer a tag types, a base struct its callbacks read past, an array sized by a count. Rust builds it too small or types it wrongly. | Such an object is allocated through the C alone, a tagged pointer is typed only where its tag is vouched for, and an object whose callbacks read more than Rust built is refused. | ASan, review |
| `hidden-dependency` | A handle, a lent pointer or a callback outlives something it depends on without showing it: a parent it points back to, a global the program may close, lent memory the C copied into a second slot. | The handle's lifetime is tied to that owner, or it keeps the owner alive; a pointer the C stores is bounded by its longest-lived reader. | ASan, Miri, review |
| `failure-leaves-state` | A failure path of the C, most often a failed allocation, leaves an object uninitialised, freed, wrongly sized or half written and still returns, sometimes reporting success. | The Rust trusts nothing the C leaves after a failure: it validates outputs again, does not reuse the object, and composes the operation itself where the C's error path is unsafe. | ASan, UBSan, review |
| `allocator-rule` | The binding vouches for a rule of alignment or allocation that some build or allocator of the C does not keep: the maximum alignment, a zero-size resize, who may free whose storage. | It vouches only for what every configured allocator guarantees, and checks alignment at each constructor that copies. | Miri, UBSan, review |
| `adoption-condition` | An adoption takes ownership without stating when the C owns the storage: a sentinel pointer at zero capacity, one element listed twice, a buffer a pool still tracks. | The contract states the exact condition, and the Rust checks it before the owner can free or resize. | ASan, review |
| `count-wrap` | A reference count the C does not check wraps once safe Rust can leak clones, and the object is freed early. | A count that can wrap within a process's lifetime is checked before each increment, and the clone fails or aborts before it wraps. | Miri, review |
| `uninitialised-as-data` | Memory the C leaves unwritten is exposed as initialised Rust data, or the argument that the C writes it is false on some path. | The Rust views it as uninitialised until every path of the C is shown to write it; an export takes raw pointers and builds no reference over memory its caller may have left unwritten. | Miri, review |
| `aliasing-at-the-boundary` | A pointer the C keeps is derived from a borrow that a later reborrow ends, or Rust holds a reference over memory the C still writes or shares. | Every pointer the C keeps is derived from the original raw pointer, and a reference is handed out only over a span no C writer or co-owner reaches. | Miri, BSan, review |

### 1.3 Threads and callbacks

| id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `unsynchronised-global` | The C reads and writes global state, or initialises it lazily on first use, without synchronisation, so that safe calls on unrelated objects race. | The Rust initialises or serialises that state before any safe call reaches it. | TSan, review |
| `assumed-locking` | A `Send` or `Sync` proof assumes the C object's own locking covers every access, but a path skips the lock, reads after releasing it, or the object has none. | Thread safety is derived from every reader and writer of each field. | review |
| `callback-state` | A trampoline mishandles a panic, a refusal or a re-entry: a stored panic goes stale or a nested call drops it, a drop panics, the C goes on after a refusal, or the callback runs under a lock of the C. | A stored panic or stop belongs to one outermost call of the C, no drop panics, and a stop is promised only where the C can be stopped. | review |

A `# Safety` contract or a `// SAFETY:` proof that is wrong in a way no pattern above names
is still a finding: a contract is derived again from every safe method that relies on it
whenever one is added.

## 2. Findings

A finding of the `ub` or `contracts` objective names its pattern, or `new`, as
[`reviewing-reports`](../../verification/reviewing/reports/SKILL.md)'s Reports section describes. A
sanitizer's false positive is no finding and names none.

A finding of a known pattern means that its statement did not let the analysis recognise
the case, or that what prevents it was not enough. A finding that is `new` is a pattern the
catalogue lacks.

## 3. Evolution

The catalogue changes only from findings a reproducer proves, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes:

- a `new` finding is proposed as a pattern once it is stated without the target's names,
  with the finding as its evidence; one that can only be stated in the target's names is
  that campaign's lesson;
- a pattern whose findings recur has its statement or its prevention sharpened, from the
  findings that escaped it; and
- a pattern no campaign has met since it was written stays: its absence is what the
  catalogue is for.

What tells whether the catalogue works is the count of findings of known patterns, over
the modules integrated since a pattern was written, taken together: it falls against the
modules before, or the catalogue is not what prevents them. One module alone tells nothing,
since modules differ. The unsafe sites the reviews read, which the count would be taken
against, are not recorded yet. The count of `new` findings tells how much of what goes wrong
the catalogue does not hold yet.

description: "The library the campaign's Rust holds C memory through, in both directions: owners, handles, lifecycle policies, status conventions, callbacks and exports. Read before writing any wrapper, owner, lifecycle strategy, callable type or export, when judging a crate for adoption, and when testing or reviewing one."

# ffibox

ffibox is the library a campaign's Rust expresses C's ownership and lifetime conventions
through, in both directions: memory C allocates, frees, copies, refcounts or locks, held
from Rust behind a safe API, and memory Rust owns that C holds, calls or reads. Its
primitives stand in for raw pointers and hand-written `Drop` impls wherever C aliases a
value; what C does not alias is plain Rust.

Its `README.md` is read in full before the first wrapper is written, and each section
below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. Which
primitive serves which C declaration, and how each is built, is those documents'. A
representation ffibox cannot express is hand-written, as its `docs/hand-written.md`
describes, with the same seam and safety-comment discipline. Its goals and non-goals,
`docs/goals.md`, are what a change to ffibox is judged against, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes.

What follows is how ffibox serves each stage: each section names the skill and section it
adds to, and states only what ffibox adds there.

## Planning

### Dependencies › Adopted crates

A candidate crate's soundness is read against the hazards `docs/goals.md`'s G9 lists,
each of which ffibox excludes from the campaign's own bindings: the crate qualifies where
its safe API excludes them too, by whatever means it uses.

## Binding workflow

### Binding workflow › Rust tree

The workspace depends on ffibox by path, on the checkout the host provides, which is on
the campaign's working branch of it, `ffibox = { path = "/crustify-rs/ffibox" }` in Crustify's image, so that
each run records its revision among its task's `revisions`. The path is the checkout's
canonical one, with no symbolic link on it, and a `[patch]` that redirects another source of
ffibox names the same: compile-fail snapshots normalize a path dependency only where the
compiler's paths match the dependency's canonical directory.
<!-- TODO: a released ffibox, as a versioned dependency, once `devel` reaches `main`.
Until then the path leaves the crate, against `bindgen`'s Layout section, and pins no
revision. -->

## Binding and porting

Binding reads `docs/ownership.md`, `docs/borrows.md`, `docs/patterns.md`,
`docs/vtables.md` and `docs/hand-written.md`; porting reads `docs/outbound.md` too.

### Binding types

A type that stays interoperable with C is bound through ffibox's primitives wherever they
apply, as `docs/ownership.md` and `docs/borrows.md` walk from its C declaration to them.

### Binding types › Safe layout

While a type keeps its C layout, `define_ctype!` mints `Foo`, `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>`,
and its owners are aliases of ffibox's owners over the policy that names its lifecycle
routines: `pub type FooBox = CBox<Foo, FooFree>;`, and `CArc<Foo, P>` for `FooArc`. A
value held inline that disposes its resources on drop is a `CVal<Foo, P>`.

### Binding symbols › Functions

A C routine's status convention becomes a `Result` through `status`, an object returned
through an out-parameter a return value through `from_c_out` or `from_raw_out`, and C's
iteration conventions iterators, as `docs/patterns.md` maps them.

### Binding symbols › Function pointers

A function pointer's callable type is a `CCallback`, where C holds it for a call or a
borrow, or a `CCallbackBox`, where C keeps it until it releases its context. Its Rust half
is a closure, a `CClosure` or a `CPayload`, which C reaches through its trampoline; its C
half is a C function with its context, a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, which Rust calls, built only
inside the crate through its `unsafe` constructor. A trampoline is the panic barrier,
`callback::barrier`, which also guards an export's body.
A struct of function pointers a library calls into, implemented by a Rust trait, is a
`CTable` whose slots `impl_cvtable!` mints, over the binding's own `unsafe impl CVtable`, as
`docs/vtables.md` describes; a table C implements is held as any other C object. A family of
hooks that carries no context is trampolines over `callback::barrier`, not a table.

### Binding symbols › Lifecycle strategies

Each lifecycle is held by the owner `docs/ownership.md` chooses for its shape, over the
policy that names its routines; a policy with state, such as an allocator context, is held
by `CBoxState`. A Rust value whose release C drives, such as a refcounted user payload, is
a `CPayload`, released through the routine it gives C.

### Porting › FFI boundary

An export gateway is built from the primitives `docs/outbound.md` chooses for what C does
with the Rust it reaches:

- the lifecycle routines C still calls on a ported type are `export_cnew!`,
  `export_cdrop!` and `export_cdupclone!` over the type's policy, which take and return
  its owners and handles;
- memory C frees comes from the allocator C frees it with: Rust's, `RustAlloc`, when C
  frees it through an exported release;
- a callback C passes an export is a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, and a value C keeps a
  `CPayload`; and
- the gateway's body runs in `callback::barrier`.

### Porting types › Structs

Until a ported struct's `port/layout`, its handles are ffibox's, as
[Binding types › Safe layout](#binding-types--safe-layout) describes; from it
on, `FooRef` and `FooMut` are aliases of native borrows. Its owners stay ffibox's until its
`port/memory`, or until its `port/layout` where that comes first, as below, their policy
calling its lifecycle routines, C's through their raw bindings until each is ported, then
the Rust ones. A `port/memory` before its `port/layout` keeps them ffibox's and changes their
policy to `RustAlloc` alone: `FooBox` becomes `CBox<Foo, RustAlloc>`, its handles unchanged,
until its `port/layout` makes it `Box<Foo>`, or `Pin<Box<Foo>>` while C keeps its address.

Between a struct's `port/layout` and its `port/memory`, its layout is native while C still
allocates or frees its storage, and ffibox's single-object owners, which hold only C-layout
types, cannot hold it. Where C releases it with its allocation family's free alone, and the
native type is not zero-sized and needs no drop (`size_of::<Foo>() != 0` and
`!core::mem::needs_drop::<Foo>()`, both asserted at compile time), and C does not keep its
address, `FooBox` is `Box<Foo, CAllocator<P>>` and a counted run of them `Vec<Foo,
CAllocator<P>>`, `P` the family's `Copy` policy with the alignment the family guarantees: an
existing `CLenAlloc` policy of the family, or one declared with `impl_clenalloc!`'s `align
=`. A box is built with `CAllocator::try_box`, which refuses an over-aligned type at compile
time and returns C's out-of-memory failure, and handed to C with
`Box::into_raw_with_allocator`; a run grows with `Vec::try_reserve`, keeping C's
out-of-memory failure, and is handed to C through `CVec::try_from` and `into_raw_parts`. A
pointer C hands back is adopted with `Box::from_raw_in`, under the conditions
`CBox::into_box`'s documentation lists, and a run with `Vec::from_raw_parts_in`, its length
as its capacity, under the allocator's fit rule. Its `port/memory` makes them `Box<Foo>` and
`Vec<Foo>`.
<!-- TODO: a native-layout struct, between its `port/layout` and its `port/memory`, that C
releases through a lifecycle routine of its own, that needs drop, whose address C keeps
(`Pin<Box<Foo, A>>` needs an allocator std does not accept yet) or that is reference-counted
(`Arc::new_in` is unstable) has no owner ffibox or std provides: it is hand-written until one
exists, or its `port/memory` is scheduled no later than its `port/layout`. -->

## Testing

### Testing › UB tests

The public seam interface ffibox exports on a type is meant to be exercised inside the
crate only, as an escape hatch for external consumers, so it gets no UB tests: a test of
it, for UB or functionality, is a unit test.

## Reviewing

Reviewing reads `docs/goals.md`.

### Reviewing › Objectives

A workset's use of ffibox's primitives is reviewed against ffibox's documentation, and its
hand-written representations against the contract ffibox would have enforced. Under `ub`,
the hazards `docs/goals.md`'s G9 lists are the checklist: each is excluded by the
primitive or the producer's contract it names, or is a finding.

### Reviewing-reports › Reports

A soundness or ergonomics gap in ffibox itself, in its safe primitives or its unsafe FFI
seams, is a defect in a tool: a proposal, as any tool defect is.
